claim: Modern humans have more fragile skeletons than other hominins.
source: Modern humans have more fragile skeletons than other hominins, which may result from physical inactivity.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on skeletal gracility

claim: Earlier onset of reproduction is associated with reduced bone mineral density (BMD) for Tsimane women.
source: Earlier onset of reproduction and shorter interbirth intervals are associated with reduced BMD for women.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Shorter interbirth intervals are associated with reduced BMD for Tsimane women.
source: Earlier onset of reproduction and shorter interbirth intervals are associated with reduced BMD for women.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Tsimane women have lower BMD than American women.
source: Tsimane BMD is lower versus Americans, but only for women, contrary to simple predictions relying on inactivity to explain skeletal fragility.
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis between Tsimane and American samples

claim: Minimal BMD differences exist between Tsimane and American men.
source: Minimal BMD differences exist between Tsimane and American men, suggesting that systemic factors other than fertility (e.g. diet) do not easily explain Tsimane women's lower BMD.
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis between Tsimane and American samples

claim: Tsimane fracture prevalence is higher than Americans.
source: Tsimane fracture prevalence is also higher versus Americans.
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis between Tsimane and American samples

claim: Lower BMD increases Tsimane fracture risk for women.
source: Lower BMD increases Tsimane fracture risk, but only for women, suggesting a role of weak bone in women's fracture etiology.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of BMD and fracture data

claim: Compared to other hominoids and extinct hominins, modern humans have postcranial skeletons that are more gracile.
source: Compared to other hominoids and extinct hominins, modern humans have postcranial skeletons that are more gracile (i.e. lower bone mass and strength for body size) (Cotter et al., 2011; Ruff et al., 2015; Ryan and Shaw, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Declining skeletal strength has been documented in the cortical structure of long bone diaphyses and in trabecular bone micro-structure.
source: Declining skeletal strength has been documented in the cortical structure of long bone diaphyses (e.g. size or shape in a cross-section) and in trabecular bone micro-structure (e.g. thickness, bone volume fraction) and is particularly evident in the later Pleistocene or Holocene (Chirchir, 2019; Chirchir et al., 2015; Ruff et al., 2015; Ryan and Shaw, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Physical inactivity is the most common explanation for skeletal fragility.
source: Physical inactivity is the most common explanation for skeletal fragility, based largely on the well-established principle that impact forces from load bearing and muscle contraction trigger bone deposition (Carter and Orr, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation and established scientific knowledge

claim: Impact forces from load bearing and muscle contraction trigger bone deposition.
source: Physical inactivity is the most common explanation for skeletal fragility, based largely on the well-established principle that impact forces from load bearing and muscle contraction trigger bone deposition (Carter and Orr, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation and established scientific knowledge

claim: Bone responds to physical activity demands by adding tissue and altering cross-sectional distribution in the direction of highest bending strains.
source: According to this principle, which has been documented in numerous studies of competitive athletes and exercise interventions (e.g. Polidoulis et al., 2012; Warden et al., 2014), and inferred from skeletal remains of prehistoric populations (e.g. Macintosh et al., 2017; Ruff et al., 2015), bone responds to physical activity demands by adding tissue and altering cross-sectional distribution in the direction of highest bending strains (i.e. change in length per unit length) (but see Demes et al., 2001; Lieberman et al., 2004; Lovejoy et al., 2003 and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The mechanical response of bone to loading is variable throughout the body, depending on types of weight-bearing activity and muscle function.
source: This mechanical response of bone to loading is variable throughout the body, depending on types of weight-bearing activity and muscle function.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Natural selection often prioritizes investments in earlier reproduction over somatic maintenance due to higher fitness gains of reproduction earlier versus later in life.
source: Due to higher fitness gains of reproduction earlier versus later in life (Williams, 1957), natural selection often prioritizes investments in earlier reproduction over somatic maintenance.
evidence: Supported by citation to life history theory

claim: Organisms may increase fertility at the expense of maintenance.
source: Organisms may thus increase fertility at the expense of maintenance (Kirkwood and Austad, 2000), and we should expect greater energetic investments in reproduction to trade-off against investments in maintenance (Stearns, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to life history theory

claim: Reproductive effort is expected to moderate effects of physical activity on adult bone strength.
source: Consistent with life history theory, reproductive effort is expected to moderate effects of physical activity on adult bone strength, which is an indicator of energetic investment in somatic maintenance.
evidence: Based on inference from life history theory

claim: Bone tissue is ideal for examining metabolic trade-offs between reproduction and maintenance.
source: Bone tissue is ideal for examining metabolic trade-offs between reproduction and maintenance.
evidence: Based on inference from the properties of bone tissue

claim: The skeleton is a general mineral reservoir for the competing metabolic demands of maternal maintenance and fetal bone accretion or lactation.
source: Constant remodeling is necessary to maintain bone strength, and the skeleton is a general mineral reservoir for the competing metabolic demands of maternal maintenance and fetal bone accretion or lactation (Stieglitz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation and established knowledge

claim: The average full-term human fetus has approximately 30 g calcium, 20 g phosphorus and 0.8 g magnesium.
source: The average full-term human fetus has ~30 g calcium, 20 g phosphorus and 0.8 g magnesium, and at least 80% of these macro-minerals are accreted in the third trimester (see Kovacs, 2016 for a comprehensive review of bone metabolism during pregnancy, lactation and post-weaning).
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review

claim: At least 80% of fetal macro-minerals are accreted in the third trimester.
source: The average full-term human fetus has ~30 g calcium, 20 g phosphorus and 0.8 g magnesium, and at least 80% of these macro-minerals are accreted in the third trimester (see Kovacs, 2016 for a comprehensive review of bone metabolism during pregnancy, lactation and post-weaning).
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review

claim: At week 24 of gestation, mean calcium transfer rate is approximately 60 mg/day for an average-sized fetus.
source: For an average-sized fetus this corresponds at week 24 of gestation to a mean calcium [phosphorus] transfer rate of ~60 mg/day [~40 mg/day] and between weeks 35–40 of 300–350 mg/day [200 mg/day].
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review (Kovacs, 2016)

claim: Between weeks 35-40 of gestation, mean calcium transfer rate is 300-350 mg/day for an average-sized fetus.
source: For an average-sized fetus this corresponds at week 24 of gestation to a mean calcium [phosphorus] transfer rate of ~60 mg/day [~40 mg/day] and between weeks 35–40 of 300–350 mg/day [200 mg/day].
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review (Kovacs, 2016)

claim: In the third trimester, hourly fetal transfers of calcium and phosphorus are between 5 and 10% of that present in maternal plasma.
source: In the third trimester, hourly fetal transfers of calcium and phosphorus are between 5 and 10% of that present in maternal plasma, which is enough to provoke maternal hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia.
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review (Kovacs, 2016)

claim: Bone turnover increases during the third trimester to create a net resorptive state.
source: Generally, patterns of bone turnover are similar comparing pre- to early pregnancy states, but turnover increases during the third trimester to create a net resorptive state.
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review (Kovacs, 2016)

claim: During the first six months postpartum, approximately 200 mg/day of calcium is secreted into human breast milk.
source: During the first six months [second six months] postpartum, ~200 mg/day [~120 mg/day] of calcium is secreted into human breast milk.
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review (Kovacs, 2016)

claim: Lactating women are in negative calcium balance, especially when milk production is elevated.
source: Analyses of bone turnover markers, bone mineral density (BMD), and bone structure by high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) suggest that lactating women are in negative calcium balance, especially when milk production is elevated.
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review (Kovacs, 2016)

claim: Longitudinal studies show mean BMD declines of 3-10% after 3-6 months of lactation.
source: Longitudinal studies show consistent declines in lactating women's BMD or bone mineral content, with mean declines of 3–10% after 3–6 months of lactation.
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review (Kovacs, 2016)

claim: The greatest BMD losses (5-10%) occur in the lumbar spine during lactation.
source: The greatest BMD losses (5–10%) occur in the lumbar spine, with modest losses (<5%) occurring at sites with less trabecular bone, and smaller losses (<2%) at sites containing mostly cortical bone.
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review (Kovacs, 2016)

claim: Peak bone mass is typically not achieved until the late 20s.
source: Peak bone mass is typically not achieved until the late 20s, so earlier pregnancy and lactation can disrupt maternal bone growth and/or mineralization (Madimenos et al., 2012; Stieglitz et al., 2015), potentially reducing peak bone mass and thus later-life bone strength (but see Chantry et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations

claim: Earlier pregnancy and lactation can disrupt maternal bone growth and/or mineralization.
source: Peak bone mass is typically not achieved until the late 20s, so earlier pregnancy and lactation can disrupt maternal bone growth and/or mineralization (Madimenos et al., 2012; Stieglitz et al., 2015), potentially reducing peak bone mass and thus later-life bone strength (but see Chantry et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Short interbirth intervals can potentially generate unbalanced cycles of maternal bone resorption and formation.
source: In addition to early onset of reproduction, short interbirth intervals (IBIs) can potentially generate unbalanced cycles of maternal bone resorption and formation, limiting maternal skeletal recovery before subsequent pregnancy (Stieglitz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation and inference

claim: For most women, lactation-associated BMD losses and micro-architectural deficits are reversed by 12 months post-weaning.
source: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry data suggest that for most women, lactation-associated BMD losses and micro-architectural deficits are reversed by 12 months post-weaning, although patterns can vary by skeletal site and most studies are conducted among well-nourished women with low fertility (Kovacs, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Restorative capacity of bone partly depends on lactation duration.
source: Restorative capacity partly depends on lactation duration; HR-pQCT studies of the radius and femur show recovery of trabecular and cortical micro-architecture in women lactating for shorter periods, but incomplete recovery in women lactating for longer periods.
evidence: Supported by citation to comprehensive review (Kovacs, 2016)

claim: Incomplete restoration of lumbar spine BMD to pre-pregnancy values by 12 months post-partum is observed among rural Gambian women practicing on-demand breastfeeding for about two years.
source: Incomplete restoration of lumbar spine BMD to pre-pregnancy values by 12 months post-partum is observed among rural Gambian women practicing on-demand breastfeeding for about two years (Jarjou et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Tsimane total fertility rate is 9 births per woman.
source: Tsimane fertility is high (total fertility rate = 9 births per woman), birth spacing is short (Stieglitz et al., 2015), breastfeeding is on-demand, effective birth control is rare, and PALs are high (Gurven et al., 2013), as is typical of other small-scale rural subsistence populations.
evidence: Supported by data from the study population

claim: Tsimane birth spacing is short.
source: Tsimane fertility is high (total fertility rate = 9 births per woman), birth spacing is short (Stieglitz et al., 2015), breastfeeding is on-demand, effective birth control is rare, and PALs are high (Gurven et al., 2013), as is typical of other small-scale rural subsistence populations.
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Tsimane physical activity levels (PALs) are high.
source: Tsimane fertility is high (total fertility rate = 9 births per woman), birth spacing is short (Stieglitz et al., 2015), breastfeeding is on-demand, effective birth control is rare, and PALs are high (Gurven et al., 2013), as is typical of other small-scale rural subsistence populations.
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: BMD accounts for approximately 70% of the variance in bone strength.
source: In a population-representative sample of adults aged 40+ years, who mostly have completed their reproduction, we utilize thoracic computed tomography (CT) to measure two primary indicators of bone strength in thoracic vertebrae: BMD, which accounts for ~70% of the variance in bone strength (NIH Consensus Development Panel on Osteoporosis Prevention, Diagnosis, and Therapy, 2001), and fracture prevalence and severity.
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Spontaneous thoracic vertebral fractures are among the most common osteoporosis-related fractures in humans.
source: We focus on thoracic vertebrae since spontaneous thoracic vertebral fractures are among the most common osteoporosis-related fractures in humans (Sambrook and Cooper, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Spontaneous thoracic vertebral fractures have not been observed in wild or captive apes, even in individuals with severe osteopenia.
source: Such fractures have not been observed in wild or captive apes, even in individuals with severe osteopenia (Gunji et al., 2003), suggesting that modern humans are more susceptible than other primates to osteoporosis-related fractures (Cotter et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Modern humans are more susceptible than other primates to osteoporosis-related fractures.
source: Such fractures have not been observed in wild or captive apes, even in individuals with severe osteopenia (Gunji et al., 2003), suggesting that modern humans are more susceptible than other primates to osteoporosis-related fractures (Cotter et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations and inference

claim: Most activities of daily living generate loads on human vertebrae.
source: Most activities of daily living, including sitting, walking, running and lifting, generate loads on human vertebrae (Myers and Wilson, 1997; Rohlmannt et al., 2001; Stewart and Hall, 2006), and thus thoracic vertebrae track mechanics of both lower and upper limbs.
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Regular breathing appears to generate intradiscal pressure and some loading in the thoracic spine.
source: Even regular breathing appears to generate intradiscal pressure and some loading in the thoracic spine (Polga et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Vertebral bodies are composed mostly of trabecular bone surrounded by a thin cortical shell.
source: Vertebral bodies, which are composed mostly of trabecular bone surrounded by a thin cortical shell, function largely as shock absorbers and can deform to a greater degree than tubular bones (Seeman, 2008); deformation facilitates spinal flexion, extension and rotation.
evidence: Supported by citation and established knowledge

claim: The major loading mode on human vertebral bodies is axially compressive.
source: The major loading mode on human vertebral bodies is axially compressive, and most axial force is carried by the trabecular bone (Myers and Wilson, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Most axial force on vertebral bodies is carried by the trabecular bone.
source: The major loading mode on human vertebral bodies is axially compressive, and most axial force is carried by the trabecular bone (Myers and Wilson, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: For many activities, the greatest compressive loads along the spine are generated in the thoracolumbar region.
source: For many activities (e.g. neutral standing, standing with weight, mild trunk flexion and extension, lifting objects above the head), the greatest compressive loads along the spine are generated in the thoracolumbar region (Bruno et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The greatest compressive vertebral loads occur during activities in which body mass or externally applied weights are shifted anteriorly.
source: The greatest compressive vertebral loads occur during activities in which body mass or externally applied weights are shifted anteriorly, such as during trunk flexion or carrying weight in front of the body (Bruno et al., 2017; Polga et al., 2004; Rohlmannt et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: The architecture of the vertebral body trabecular bone consists of thick vertical plates and columns supported by thinner horizontal trabeculae.
source: To accommodate forces, the architecture of the vertebral body trabecular bone consists of thick vertical plates and columns supported by thinner horizontal trabeculae.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: With age, vertical trabecular plates are successively perforated during remodeling and converted into columns, whereas horizontal trabeculae perforate and disappear.
source: This trabecular structure changes with age, such that vertical plates are successively perforated during remodeling and converted into columns, whereas horizontal trabeculae perforate and disappear (Mosekilde et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Age-related trabecular structural changes can result in vertebral strength declines that are greater than predicted from bone mass estimation alone.
source: These age-related trabecular structural changes can result in vertebral strength declines that are greater than predicted from bone mass estimation alone.
evidence: Based on inference from cited research on trabecular changes

claim: Vertebral strength is compromised more by loss of trabecular connectivity than by trabecular thinning.
source: Vertebral strength is compromised more by loss of trabecular connectivity than by trabecular thinning, and women are more susceptible than men to age-related horizontal trabecular perforation and disappearance (Mosekilde, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Women are more susceptible than men to age-related horizontal trabecular perforation and disappearance.
source: Vertebral strength is compromised more by loss of trabecular connectivity than by trabecular thinning, and women are more susceptible than men to age-related horizontal trabecular perforation and disappearance (Mosekilde, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Earlier age at first birth is associated with reduced BMD among Tsimane women (Std. β=0.099, p=0.036).
source: Earlier age at first birth is associated with reduced BMD (Std. βAge at 1st birth [years, logged]=0.099, p=0.036, controlling for age and fat-free mass, adj. R2 = 0.51, n = 213; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: There is a BMD difference of 0.57 SDs for Tsimane women with maximum versus minimum age at first birth (37 versus 12 years).
source: Back-transforming logged age at first birth values into observed values and holding controls at sample means, there is a BMD difference of 0.57 SDs for women with maximum versus minimum age at first birth (37 versus 12 years, respectively).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: Parity is not associated with BMD among Tsimane women controlling for age at first birth, age and fat-free mass.
source: Parity (continuously or categorically operationalized) is not associated with BMD controlling for age at first birth, age and fat-free mass (Appendix 1—table 2), nor does parity interact with any indicator of reproductive effort to predict BMD.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: Shorter mean interbirth interval (<29.7 months) is associated with lower BMD among Tsimane women (Std. β=-0.201, p=0.032).
source: Shorter mean IBI (<29.7 months) is associated with lower BMD (Std. βShorter mean IBI=-0.201, p=0.032, controlling for age at first birth, age and fat-free mass, adj. R2 = 0.52; Appendix 1—tables 3–4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: Mean interbirth interval interacts with age at first birth to predict BMD among Tsimane women.
source: Mean IBI also interacts with age at first birth: BMD is 0.28 SDs higher for women with longer mean IBI and later age at first birth versus women with shorter mean IBI and earlier age at first birth (interaction p=0.027, controlling for age and fat-free mass; see Figure 1 and Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1

claim: Age-standardized mean BMD is 8.9% lower for Tsimane women than American women.
source: For women, age-standardized mean BMD is 8.9% lower for Tsimane than Americans (Figure 2; Appendix 1—table 7).
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: BMD is significantly lower for Tsimane women than American women at all ages.
source: BMD is significantly lower (all p's < 0.01) for Tsimane than Americans at all ages, and this population-level difference increases with age in the cross-section.
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis

claim: Mean BMD for Tsimane women is 5.6% lower than age-matched Americans aged 40-49 years.
source: Mean BMD for Tsimane women is 5.6% lower than age-matched Americans aged 40–49 years, 9.8% lower for ages 50–59, 13.7% lower for ages 60–69, and 18.8% lower for women aged 70+.
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis

claim: Age-standardized mean BMD is 0.24% lower for Tsimane men than American men.
source: For men, age-standardized mean BMD is 0.24% lower for Tsimane than Americans.
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis

claim: Tsimane men aged 50-59 have 4% higher mean BMD than age-matched Americans (p=0.027).
source: Tsimane men aged 50–59 have 4% higher mean BMD (p=0.027) than age-matched Americans.
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis

claim: Age-standardized prevalence of any thoracic vertebral fracture for Tsimane women is 18% and for American women is 9%.
source: For women, age-standardized prevalence of any thoracic vertebral fracture (i.e. grade ≥1; including mild, moderate or severe) for Tsimane and Americans is 18% and 9%, respectively (adjusted RRTsimane [vs. US]=1.81, 95% CI: 1.16–2.83, p=0.009, controlling for age, n = 491; see Figure 3 and Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: Using a more conservative fracture definition (grade ≥2), age-standardized prevalence for Tsimane women is 6% and for American women is 2%.
source: Using a more conservative fracture definition (i.e. grade ≥2; including only moderate or severe), age-standardized prevalence for Tsimane and Americans is 6% and 2%, respectively (adjusted RRTsimane [vs. US]=2.69, 95% CI: 1.07–6.75, p=0.035; Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis

claim: Age-standardized prevalence of any thoracic vertebral fracture for Tsimane men is 36% and for American men is 11%.
source: For men, age-standardized prevalence of any fracture for Tsimane and Americans is 36% and 11%, respectively (adjusted RRTsimane [vs. US]=3.30, 95% CI: 2.26–4.82, p<0.001, n = 524; Appendix 1—table 8), and using a more conservative fracture definition, 10% and 2%, respectively (adjusted RRTsimane [vs. US]=3.79, 95% CI: 1.78–8.09, p=0.001; Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis

claim: Tsimane are significantly more likely than Americans to present moderate (grade 2) fracture for both sexes.
source: For both sexes, Tsimane are significantly more likely than Americans to present moderate (i.e. grade 2) but not severe (grade 3) fracture (Appendix 1—tables 10–11).
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis

claim: Tsimane men but not women are significantly more likely than Americans to present borderline deformity (grade 0.5) and mild fracture (grade 1).
source: Tsimane men but not women are significantly more likely than Americans to present borderline deformity (grade 0.5) and mild fracture (grade 1).
evidence: Supported by comparative data analysis

claim: Tsimane women with thoracic vertebral fracture have lower BMD (0.46 SDs; p=0.005) than women without fracture.
source: Tsimane women with thoracic vertebral fracture (grade ≥1) have lower BMD (0.46 SDs; p=0.005), higher parity (0.25 SDs; p=0.071) and shorter mean IBI (0.22 SDs; p=0.011) than women without fracture (Appendix 1—table 12).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: Tsimane women with thoracic vertebral fracture have shorter mean interbirth interval (0.22 SDs; p=0.011) than women without fracture.
source: Tsimane women with thoracic vertebral fracture (grade ≥1) have lower BMD (0.46 SDs; p=0.005), higher parity (0.25 SDs; p=0.071) and shorter mean IBI (0.22 SDs; p=0.011) than women without fracture (Appendix 1—table 12).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: Tsimane women's BMD is inversely associated with fracture risk (adjusted RR per SD increase = 0.542, 95% CI: 0.352-0.837, p=0.006).
source: Women's BMD is inversely associated with fracture risk (adjusted RRBMD per SD increase = 0.542, 95% CI: 0.352–0.837, p=0.006, controlling for age, height and fat mass, n = 219); this association remains (adjusted RRBMD = 0.540, 95% CI: 0.345–0.845, p=0.007; Figure 4) after adding to the model mean IBI, which is also inversely associated with fracture risk (adjusted RRMean IBI per SD increase = 0.379, 95% CI: 0.165–0.866, p=0.021; Appendix 1—table 13: Model 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Tsimane women's mean interbirth interval is inversely associated with fracture risk (adjusted RR per SD increase = 0.379, 95% CI: 0.165-0.866, p=0.021).
source: Women's BMD is inversely associated with fracture risk (adjusted RRBMD per SD increase = 0.542, 95% CI: 0.352–0.837, p=0.006, controlling for age, height and fat mass, n = 219); this association remains (adjusted RRBMD = 0.540, 95% CI: 0.345–0.845, p=0.007; Figure 4) after adding to the model mean IBI, which is also inversely associated with fracture risk (adjusted RRMean IBI per SD increase = 0.379, 95% CI: 0.165–0.866, p=0.021; Appendix 1—table 13: Model 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: The inverse association between Tsimane women's BMD and fracture risk strengthens with higher fracture grades.
source: The inverse association between women's BMD and fracture risk strengthens with higher fracture grades (Appendix 1—table 14), whereas the inverse association between mean IBI and fracture risk is strongest for mild (i.e. grade 1) fracture.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: Tsimane men with fracture are shorter (0.23 SDs; p=0.038) than men without fracture.
source: Tsimane men with fracture are shorter (0.23 SDs; p=0.038), have higher adiposity (0.37 SDs; p=0.025) and have higher BMI (0.34 SDs; p=0.012) than men without fracture (Appendix 1—table 15).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: Tsimane men with fracture have higher adiposity (0.37 SDs; p=0.025) than men without fracture.
source: Tsimane men with fracture are shorter (0.23 SDs; p=0.038), have higher adiposity (0.37 SDs; p=0.025) and have higher BMI (0.34 SDs; p=0.012) than men without fracture (Appendix 1—table 15).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: There is no significant difference in BMD between Tsimane men without versus with fracture.
source: But unlike women, there is no significant difference in BMD between men without versus with fracture, and men's BMD is not associated with risk of any fracture (adjusted RRBMD per SD increase = 1.046, 95% CI: 0.862–1.269, p=0.650, controlling for age, height and fat mass, n = 227; Appendix 1—table 16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: Tsimane men's BMD is not associated with risk of any fracture (adjusted RR per SD increase = 1.046, 95% CI: 0.862-1.269, p=0.650).
source: But unlike women, there is no significant difference in BMD between men without versus with fracture, and men's BMD is not associated with risk of any fracture (adjusted RRBMD per SD increase = 1.046, 95% CI: 0.862–1.269, p=0.650, controlling for age, height and fat mass, n = 227; Appendix 1—table 16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of study data

claim: Tsimane men's BMD is inversely associated with risk of borderline (grade 0.5) deformity.
source: Men's BMD is, however, inversely associated with risk of borderline (i.e. grade 0.5) deformity (Appendix 1—table 17; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: The results are consistent with a life history trade-off between reproductive effort and somatic maintenance.
source: These results are consistent with a life history trade-off between reproductive effort and somatic maintenance (Kirkwood and Austad, 2000; Stearns, 1992; Stieglitz et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on inference from the study results and life history theory

claim: Maternal physiology uniquely responds to the greater mineral demands of pregnancy and lactation by mobilizing skeletal mineral stores.
source: Maternal physiology uniquely responds to the greater mineral demands of pregnancy and lactation by mobilizing skeletal mineral stores (Kovacs, 2016; Nelson et al., 2002; Prentice, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: In energy-limited settings, earlier age at first birth and shorter birth spacing can potentially reduce peak bone mass and generate unbalanced cycles of bone resorption and formation.
source: But in energy-limited settings (due to high energy expenditure relative to consumption), earlier age at first birth and shorter birth spacing can potentially reduce peak bone mass and generate unbalanced cycles of bone resorption and formation, compromising bone strength long before menopause.
evidence: Based on inference from physiological mechanisms and study context

claim: Indirect negative effects of reproductive effort on bone strength are possible via reductions in women's physical activity levels and mechanical loading on bone.
source: In addition to direct negative effects of reproductive effort on bone strength, indirect negative effects are possible via reductions in women's PALs and mechanical loading on bone, given nursing women's reduced food acquisition efforts relative to non-nursing women (cf. Hurtado et al., 1992).
evidence: Based on inference and citation

claim: High-impact and high-magnitude loadings are especially effective at preserving women's BMD at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip.
source: Tsimane women's participation in certain subsistence activities ostensibly entailing high-impact and high-magnitude loadings (e.g. rice-pounding using thick wooden bats) may be curtailed during pregnancy and early lactation; meta analyses of controlled exercise trials indicate that high-impact and high-magnitude loadings are especially effective at preserving women's BMD at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip (Martyn-St James and Carroll, 2009; Martyn-St James and Carroll, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to meta-analyses

claim: Dietary or other systemic population-level differences do not easily explain Tsimane women's lower BMD because such systemic factors should affect both sexes.
source: Dietary or other systemic population-level differences (e.g. in infectious burden) do not easily explain Tsimane women's lower BMD because such systemic factors should affect both sexes.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the sex-specific pattern of results

claim: Tsimane mean daily per-capita energy, protein and carbohydrate intake exceeds that of Americans for both sexes.
source: Recent dietary analyses of Tsimane and Americans (NHANES) based on 24 hr dietary recalls indicate minor sex differences in proportional macronutrient intake for both populations (Kraft et al., 2018). In absolute terms, Tsimane mean daily per-capita energy, protein and carbohydrate intake actually exceeds that of Americans for both sexes, as does Tsimane intake of the bone-forming minerals magnesium, phosphorus and zinc.
evidence: Supported by citation to dietary analysis

claim: Tsimane intake of the bone-forming minerals magnesium, phosphorus and zinc exceeds that of Americans for both sexes.
source: Recent dietary analyses of Tsimane and Americans (NHANES) based on 24 hr dietary recalls indicate minor sex differences in proportional macronutrient intake for both populations (Kraft et al., 2018). In absolute terms, Tsimane mean daily per-capita energy, protein and carbohydrate intake actually exceeds that of Americans for both sexes, as does Tsimane intake of the bone-forming minerals magnesium, phosphorus and zinc.
evidence: Supported by citation to dietary analysis

claim: Energetic limitation and greater immune activation from high pathogen exposure partly explain why mean PALs above those of industrialized societies do not inevitably yield elevated peak bone mass or protect against age-related bone loss for either sex among Tsimane.
source: Nevertheless, prior Tsimane research indicates that energetic limitation and greater immune activation from high pathogen exposure partly explain why mean PALs above those of industrialized societies do not inevitably yield elevated peak bone mass or protect against age-related bone loss for either sex (Stieglitz et al., 2015; Stieglitz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Reduced calcaneal strength for Tsimane versus American women is already apparent in the 20s, with population-level differences increasing with age.
source: In a prior cross-sectional study of women utilizing ultrasound, we found reduced calcaneal strength for Tsimane versus Americans that is already apparent in the 20s, with population-level differences increasing with age (Stieglitz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Sex-specific costs of reproduction contribute to skeletal sexual dimorphism.
source: Between- and within-population analyses in the present study suggest that sex-specific costs of reproduction contribute to skeletal sexual dimorphism, and that sexually dimorphic responses to reproduction manifest early in adulthood, depending on age at first birth and birth spacing (Madimenos et al., 2012; Stieglitz et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on inference from study results and citations

claim: Sexually dimorphic responses to reproduction manifest early in adulthood, depending on age at first birth and birth spacing.
source: Between- and within-population analyses in the present study suggest that sex-specific costs of reproduction contribute to skeletal sexual dimorphism, and that sexually dimorphic responses to reproduction manifest early in adulthood, depending on age at first birth and birth spacing (Madimenos et al., 2012; Stieglitz et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on inference from study results and citations

claim: There is relatively scant bio-archaeological evidence of osteoporotic fracture prior to industrialization.
source: Higher fracture prevalence among Tsimane versus Americans is noteworthy in light of relatively scant bio-archaeological evidence of osteoporotic fracture prior to industrialization (Agarwal, 2008; Curate et al., 2010) and evidence of increasing age-specific osteoporotic fracture incidence rates over time in Western populations (Cooper et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Age-specific osteoporotic fracture incidence rates have increased over time in Western populations.
source: Higher fracture prevalence among Tsimane versus Americans is noteworthy in light of relatively scant bio-archaeological evidence of osteoporotic fracture prior to industrialization (Agarwal, 2008; Curate et al., 2010) and evidence of increasing age-specific osteoporotic fracture incidence rates over time in Western populations (Cooper et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The fact that Tsimane women's vertebral BMD is inversely associated with vertebral fracture risk suggests a major role of compromised bone strength in precipitating fracture, rather than traumatic injury of otherwise healthy bone.
source: The fact that Tsimane women's vertebral BMD is inversely associated with vertebral fracture risk (cf. Mays, 1996) (Figure 4) suggests a major role of compromised bone strength in precipitating fracture, rather than traumatic injury of otherwise healthy bone.
evidence: Based on inference from the statistical association shown in Figure 4

claim: For Tsimane men, it is likely that trauma plays a major role in precipitating fracture.
source: For Tsimane men, it is likely that trauma plays a major role in precipitating fracture due to: 1) a weak association between BMD and fracture risk (Figure 4); 2) a high fracture prevalence relative to a comparative American sample (Figure 3) despite minimal BMD differences (Figure 2); and our anecdotal observations of high levels of mechanical stress on Tsimane men's vertebrae from frequent heavy load carrying (e.g. of hunted game, timber for constructing houses).
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including data shown in Figures 2-4 and anecdotal observations

claim: The fact that Tsimane women's shorter interbirth intervals predict increased fracture risk even after adjusting for BMD suggests that shorter interbirth intervals compromise multiple aspects of vertebral micro-architecture.
source: The fact that Tsimane women's shorter IBIs predict increased fracture risk even after adjusting for BMD, which also remains a significant predictor (Appendix 1—table 13–14), suggests that shorter IBIs compromise multiple aspects of vertebral micro-architecture (e.g. trabecular thickness or connectivity density), although further research is needed to examine this possibility.
evidence: Based on inference from statistical results, with acknowledgment of speculation

claim: It has been hypothesized that subsistence transition from hunting and gathering to more sedentary agriculture caused reductions in mechanical loading on bone and physical activity levels, leading to modern human skeletal gracilization.
source: It has been hypothesized that subsistence transition from hunting and gathering to more sedentary agriculture, and increasing reliance on labor-saving technology, caused reductions in mechanical loading on bone and PALs, leading to modern human skeletal gracilization (Chirchir, 2019; Chirchir et al., 2015; Chirchir et al., 2017; Ruff et al., 2015; Ryan and Shaw, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior hypotheses

claim: Comparisons of skeletal remains of hunter-gatherers and agriculturalists indicate among agriculturalists reduced femoral strength.
source: Nevertheless, comparisons of skeletal remains of hunter-gatherers and either full- or part-time agriculturalists indicate among agriculturalists reduced femoral strength, as indicated by trabecular bone structure or external size dimensions (Larsen, 1981; Ryan and Shaw, 2015), and accelerated age-related decline in radial bone mineral content (Perzigian, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Evidence that agriculturalists are more sedentary than hunter-gatherers is not particularly strong.
source: Evidence that agriculturalists are more sedentary than hunter-gatherers is not particularly strong: PALs and time allocation to work vary substantially within a subsistence regime, and both measures are actually higher among agriculturalists (Gurven et al., 2013; Leonard, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Physical activity levels and time allocation to work are actually higher among agriculturalists than hunter-gatherers.
source: Evidence that agriculturalists are more sedentary than hunter-gatherers is not particularly strong: PALs and time allocation to work vary substantially within a subsistence regime, and both measures are actually higher among agriculturalists (Gurven et al., 2013; Leonard, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Children in agricultural societies generally begin work earlier than hunter-gatherer children.
source: Moreover, children in agricultural societies generally begin work earlier than hunter-gatherer children (Kramer, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Higher physical activity levels in childhood and early adulthood, particularly for higher-impact activities producing high peak stresses, increase peak bone mass, size and later-life bone strength.
source: This is significant because higher PALs in childhood and early adulthood, particularly for higher-impact activities producing high peak stresses, increase peak bone mass, size and later-life bone strength (e.g. see Warden et al., 2014 and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: In a prospective Tsimane study, time spent in horticulture positively predicted ultrasound-derived indicators of radial strength.
source: Furthermore, in a prospective Tsimane study we found that time spent in horticulture positively predicted ultrasound-derived indicators of radial strength (Stieglitz et al., 2017), whereas tibial strength was not predicted by extent of involvement in any subsistence activity including hunting.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Fertility increases were associated with subsistence transition from foraging to farming.
source: Our results instead suggest that fertility increases associated with subsistence transition from foraging to farming (Bentley et al., 1993) contributed to modern human skeletal gracility, particularly for women.
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Fertility increases associated with subsistence transition from foraging to farming contributed to modern human skeletal gracility, particularly for women.
source: Our results instead suggest that fertility increases associated with subsistence transition from foraging to farming (Bentley et al., 1993) contributed to modern human skeletal gracility, particularly for women.
evidence: Based on inference from study results and citation

claim: Women's skeletons were especially susceptible to gracilization during subsistence transition from foraging to farming in light of the associated increases in fertility.
source: Regardless of proximate fertility determinants, given the trade-off between energetic investment in reproduction and somatic maintenance, our results suggest that women's skeletons were especially susceptible to gracilization during subsistence transition from foraging to farming in light of the associated increases in fertility, and reduced mobility resulting from increased fertility (cf. Hurtado et al., 1992).
evidence: Based on inference from study results and citations

claim: Any explanation solely resting on changes in reproductive effort cannot explain skeletal gracilization observed in both sexes during subsistence transition.
source: Nevertheless, since skeletal gracilization is observed in both sexes during this subsistence transition (Ruff et al., 2015), any explanation solely resting on changes in reproductive effort cannot explain these morphological changes in men.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the observation of gracilization in both sexes

claim: All Tsimane women breastfeed their infants.
source: However, all Tsimane women breastfeed their infants and it is common for women to breastfeed exclusively for about four months (no study participant bottle fed an infant).
evidence: Based on observational data from the study population

claim: It is common for Tsimane women to breastfeed exclusively for about four months.
source: However, all Tsimane women breastfeed their infants and it is common for women to breastfeed exclusively for about four months (no study participant bottle fed an infant).
evidence: Based on observational data from the study population

claim: Bone strength indicators such as BMD and fracture are heritable.
source: Bone strength indicators such as BMD and fracture are heritable and the frequency of alleles affecting BMD differs between ethnically distinct populations (see Wallace et al., 2016 and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The frequency of alleles affecting BMD differs between ethnically distinct populations.
source: Bone strength indicators such as BMD and fracture are heritable and the frequency of alleles affecting BMD differs between ethnically distinct populations (see Wallace et al., 2016 and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: There is little evidence that heterogeneity in bone strength between populations is due to stochastic genetic diversity.
source: But while genetic factors can account for a sizable portion of variance in bone strength within populations, there is little evidence that heterogeneity in bone strength between populations is due to stochastic genetic diversity.
evidence: Based on inference from the literature on genetic factors and bone strength

claim: Tsimane forager-horticulturalists live in more than 90 villages in lowland Bolivia.
source: Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of lowland Bolivia are semi-sedentary and live in >90 villages.
evidence: Based on descriptive data about the study population

claim: Tsimane diet consists of 62% cultigens, 16% freshwater fish, 14% meat from hunting and domesticated animals, 8% market foods, and less than 1% wild fruit and vegetables.
source: Their diet consists of cultigens grown in small swiddens (62% of total calories; mostly plantains [60% of cultigen-derived calories], rice, sweet manioc and corn), freshwater fish (16%), meat from hunting and domesticated animals (14%), market foods (8%; mostly pasta [55% of market-derived calories]) and wild fruit and vegetables (<1%) (Kraft et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to dietary analysis

claim: Tsimane calcium intake is approximately 240 mg/day.
source: Relative to Western dietary recommendations calcium intake is low (~240 mg/day), but intake of other bone-forming minerals is ample (magnesium: ~525 mg/day; zinc: ~14 mg/day) or high (phosphorus: ~1,550 mg/day).
evidence: Based on dietary data from the study population

claim: Tsimane magnesium intake is approximately 525 mg/day.
source: Relative to Western dietary recommendations calcium intake is low (~240 mg/day), but intake of other bone-forming minerals is ample (magnesium: ~525 mg/day; zinc: ~14 mg/day) or high (phosphorus: ~1,550 mg/day).
evidence: Based on dietary data from the study population

claim: Tsimane phosphorus intake is approximately 1,550 mg/day.
source: Relative to Western dietary recommendations calcium intake is low (~240 mg/day), but intake of other bone-forming minerals is ample (magnesium: ~525 mg/day; zinc: ~14 mg/day) or high (phosphorus: ~1,550 mg/day).
evidence: Based on dietary data from the study population

claim: Tsimane women's physical activity level is in the 'moderate to active' range (PAL = 1.7-1.9) and remains constant throughout adulthood.
source: Women's PAL is in the 'moderate to active' range (PAL = 1.7–1.9) and remains constant throughout adulthood.
evidence: Based on data from the study population

claim: Tsimane men's physical activity level is 'vigorously active' (PAL = 2.0-2.2), and declines by 10-20% from the peak in the late 20s to older adulthood (age 60+ years).
source: Men's PAL is 'vigorously active' (PAL = 2.0–2.2), and declines by 10–20% from the peak (in the late 20s) to older adulthood (age 60+ years) (Gurven et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The Tsimane sample includes 507 individuals aged 40+ years (48% female; age range: 41-94 years).
source: The Tsimane sample includes all individuals who met the inclusion criteria of self-identifying as Tsimane and who were aged 40+ years (n = 507; 48% female; age range: 41–94 years; see Appendix for additional details and Appendix 1—table 18 for descriptives of all study variables).
evidence: Based on descriptive data about the study sample

claim: 185 of the 245 participating Tsimane women (76%) were post-menopausal.
source: 185 of the 245 participating women (76%) were post-menopausal.
evidence: Based on descriptive data about the study sample

claim: No Tsimane study participant reported ever using hormonal contraception or dietary supplements with consistency.
source: No participant reported ever using hormonal contraception or dietary supplements with consistency.
evidence: Based on self-reported data from study participants

claim: CT-derived BMD estimates can be obtained with and without calibration phantoms.
source: CT-derived BMD estimates can be obtained with and without calibration phantoms.
evidence: Based on established CT methodology

claim: Phantomless BMD estimates correlate strongly (Pearson r = 0.99) with standard phantom-based CT BMD estimates.
source: Phantomless BMD estimates correlate strongly (Pearson r = 0.99) with standard phantom-based CT BMD estimates (Budoff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: CT-derived thoracic vertebral BMD is strongly positively correlated (Pearson r's > 0.9) with lumbar vertebral BMD.
source: This BMD measure is strongly positively correlated (Pearson r's > 0.9) with lumbar vertebral BMD (Budoff et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Genant's semi-quantitative technique provides highly reproducible diagnosis of vertebral fractures.
source: While there is no consensus regarding the radiologic definition of vertebral fracture, the GST provides highly reproducible diagnosis of fractures, is the current clinical technique of choice for diagnosing fracture, and is the most widely used technique for identifying fracture (Shepherd et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Genant's semi-quantitative technique is the current clinical technique of choice for diagnosing vertebral fracture.
source: While there is no consensus regarding the radiologic definition of vertebral fracture, the GST provides highly reproducible diagnosis of fractures, is the current clinical technique of choice for diagnosing fracture, and is the most widely used technique for identifying fracture (Shepherd et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation
